$$\vec E^{(l)}=\Bigl(W^{(l)\top}\vec E^{(l+1)}\Bigr)\odot g'\bigl(\vec z^{(l)}\bigr)$$

Neural networks: the backward pass, the activation, and the step size

One equation propagates blame backwards through a network. Everything else is a consequence of it: why sigmoid stalls, why ReLU dies, and why the learning rate cannot stay fixed.

Forward pass & backpropagation Activation functions Learning rate decay

Part A
The forward pass
1

The artificial neuron

Two operations in sequence — a weighted sum, then a function applied to it. Everything in these notes follows from keeping those two separate.

A neuron receives inputs \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_d\), scales each by its own weight, and adds the results. That single number is the pre-activation:

$$z=\sum_{i=0}^{d} w_i x_i = w^{\top}x$$

The input \(x_0\) is fixed at \(1\), so \(w_0\) acts as a bias that shifts \(z\) without depending on the data. The pre-activation is then passed through an activation function \(g\), giving the neuron's output:

$$a = g(z) = g\!\left(w^{\top}x\right)$$

\(g\) is an activation function. Examples:

  • Sigmoid
  • Tanh
  • ReLU
These functions output a continuous value, and the useful question is not whether the neuron fired but how strongly, and — far more importantly for training — how sensitive that output is to a small change in \(z\). That sensitivity is \(g'(z)\), and blocks 5 to 12 show it appearing in every weight update in the network.

Notation used throughout

A superscript \((l)\) in round brackets indexes a layer, never a power: \(a^{(2)}\) is the activation vector of layer 2, while \(a^2\) would be a square. Subscripts index units within a layer. \(w^{(l)}_{ij}\) is the weight from unit \(j\) in layer \(l\) to unit \(i\) in layer \(l+1\) — note that the destination index comes first, which is what makes the matrix form in block 10 come out without a transpose.

\(J\) is the cost, \(g\) an activation function, \(\alpha\) the learning rate, and \(\odot\) the element-wise product defined in block 9.

2

Why a non-linearity is compulsory

Suppose we drop \(g\) and let every layer be purely linear. Two layers then compute

$$a^{(3)} = W^{(2)}\left(W^{(1)}a^{(1)}\right) = \left(W^{(2)}W^{(1)}\right)a^{(1)} = \tilde W a^{(1)}$$

The product \(W^{(2)}W^{(1)}\) is just another matrix. A hundred stacked linear layers collapse in exactly the same way into a single matrix \(\tilde W\), so the network can only ever represent a linear map — no matter how many layers or units it has. All the extra parameters buy nothing; they are redundant re-parameterisations of one linear function.

This is what makes the choice of \(g\) consequential rather than cosmetic. It also sets a floor on what \(g\) must provide: it has to be non-linear, and — because backpropagation needs \(g'\) — it has to be differentiable almost everywhere.

How much does one hidden layer buy?

A great deal. The universal approximation theorem says that a network with a single hidden layer and a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to any accuracy, given enough hidden units. With ReLU the construction is easy to picture: each unit contributes one hinge, and enough hinges approximate any curve.

If one hidden layer is already universal, why does anyone build deep networks?

Because "enough hidden units" can mean exponentially many. Certain functions that a deep network represents with \(O(n)\) units need \(O(2^n)\) units in a shallow one — depth lets features be reused and composed rather than enumerated. The theorem is about representability, not about parameter efficiency or learnability.

3

Layers, shapes and parameter counts

A feedforward network is neurons arranged in layers, each layer reading only the one before it.

The input layer holds the data and does no computation, so a network described as having "two hidden layers" has three weight matrices. Layers between the input and output are hidden in the sense that the training data says nothing about what they should contain — their values are whatever the optimisation makes them.

Counting parameters between two layers

With \(m\) units in layer \(l\) and \(n\) units in layer \(l+1\), every pair is connected, giving \(m \times n\) weights, plus one bias per receiving unit:

$$\bigl|\text{parameters}\bigr| = m\,n + n = n\,(m+1)$$
LayerUnitsWeight matrix \(W^{(l)}\)WeightsBiasesTotal
Input4———0
Hidden 15\(5\times4\)20525
Hidden 25\(5\times5\)25530
Output3\(3\times5\)15318
Network601373

Every one of those 73 numbers needs a partial derivative \(\partial J/\partial w\) on every training step. Computing them one at a time by re-running the network is hopeless; backpropagation computes all of them in a single backward sweep.

4

The forward pass in matrix form

For one layer, with \(\vec a^{(l)}\) of length \(m\) and \(\vec a^{(l+1)}\) of length \(n\):

$$\vec z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l)}\vec a^{(l)} + \vec b^{(l)}, \qquad \vec a^{(l+1)} = g\!\left(\vec z^{(l+1)}\right)$$
\(W^{(l)}\) is \((n\times m)\), \(\;\vec a^{(l)}\) is \((m\times1)\), \(\;\vec b^{(l)}\) and \(\vec z^{(l+1)}\) are \((n\times1)\)

\(g\) is applied element-wise: each unit passes its own \(z\) through the same scalar function, independently of its neighbours. Softmax (block 19) is the one common exception, and that exception is exactly why it needs separate treatment.

Running this from \(\vec a^{(1)} = \vec x\) to the output layer gives the prediction \(\hat y = \vec a^{(L)}\). The full forward pass for the four-layer network above is

$$\vec x = \vec a^{(1)} \;\longrightarrow\; \vec z^{(2)},\,$$ $$\vec a^{(2)} \;\longrightarrow\; \vec z^{(3)},\,$$ $$\vec a^{(3)} \;\longrightarrow\; \vec z^{(4)},\,$$ $$ \vec a^{(4)} = \hat y \;\longrightarrow\; J$$

At this point every activation in the network is known — but nothing is known about how changing a weight would change \(J\) (the loss function). That derivative is what gradient descent needs:

$$w^{(k+1)} = w^{(k)} - \alpha\,\nabla_w J$$

Supplying \(\nabla_w J\) for every weight in the network is the entire job of the backward pass.

Part B
Backpropagation
5

What the backward pass has to compute

One number per weight, and a way of getting all of them without redoing the same work for each.

Gradient descent needs \(\partial J/\partial w\) for every weight. The obstacle is that a weight in an early layer affects \(J\) only through a long chain of intermediate quantities, and different weights share most of that chain. Backpropagation exploits the sharing: it computes each shared piece once, stores it, and reuses it.

The quantity worth storing turns out to be the derivative of the cost with respect to a layer's pre-activation. We call it the error signal:

$$E^{(l)} \;\equiv\; \frac{\partial J}{\partial z^{(l)}}$$

Once \(E^{(l)}\) is known for a layer, two things follow immediately:

  • The gradient of every weight feeding into that layer
  • The error signal of the layer before it
Those are the two recursions of block 8.

6

Assigning blame: the assembly line

A fault is observed only at the end of the line:

  • The Analogy: You only realize the car's doors don't close once the car is completely finished.
  • The ML Reality: In a neural network, you don't know if the internal layers are doing a good job until the very end, when the network makes its final prediction and you compare it to the actual answer (calculating the final Loss or Error).
To fix it you need to know:how much each earlier stage contributed , and the answer depends on two things:
  • How strongly that stage influences the next one
    • The Analogy: If the Body Shop welds the frame even slightly crooked, the Assembly Line will have a massive problem fitting the doors later. Therefore, the Body Shop has a very strong influence and deserves a large share of the blame.
    • The ML Reality: This represents the weights connecting the neurons. If the connection (weight) between two layers is very large, a tiny change in the earlier layer will cause a massive change in the later layer.
  • How sensitive that stage is to being adjusted at all
    • The Analogy: If you tell a specific shop they messed up, how easily can they actually change their machines to fix it? Are their machines flexible, or are they locked into one setting?
    • The ML Reality: This represents the derivative of the activation function at a specific neuron. It asks: if we tweak this neuron's input just a little bit, will its output actually change?
A stage that is already jammed at its limit cannot be blamed usefully, however much it influenced the outcome.

  • The Analogy: Imagine the Press Shop machines are already running at absolute maximum physical pressure (100%). Even if their output is causing the doors to not fit, telling them to "press harder" won't do anything because the machine is maxed out. Since adjusting them is impossible, assigning them blame is useless.
  • The ML Reality: This perfectly describes a saturated neuron, which leads to the vanishing gradient problem. For example, if a neuron uses a Sigmoid activation function and its input is extremely high, it outputs a flat 1.0. Its derivative (sensitivity) becomes zero. Because it is "jammed at its limit," the algorithm cannot update its weights to fix the final error, no matter how badly that neuron is messing up the network.
On the assembly lineIn the networkWhat it does
Fault found at final inspection\(\vec E^{(l+1)}\)The error signal arriving from the next layer
Blame split by how much each stage influenced the next\(W^{(l)\top}\vec E^{(l+1)}\)Routes blame backwards in proportion to the connecting weights
Some stages are more adjustable than others\(g'\!\left(\vec z^{(l)}\right)\)Scales blame by how responsive each unit currently is
Blame finally attached to each stage\(\vec E^{(l)}\)The error signal for this layer

The second and third rows are the two failure modes of Part C in disguise. If the weights are small, blame shrinks as it travels back. If \(g'\) is near zero — a saturated sigmoid, a dead ReLU — the stage absorbs the blame and passes nothing on. Either way, the early stages never learn what they did wrong.

7

The chain rule on a scalar chain

Take the four-stage chain of block 5, with all quantities scalar:

Linear stepNon-linear stepEnds
\(z^{(2)} = w^{(1)}a^{(1)}\)\(a^{(2)} = g\!\left(z^{(2)}\right)\)\(a^{(1)} = x\)
\(z^{(3)} = w^{(2)}a^{(2)}\)\(a^{(3)} = g\!\left(z^{(3)}\right)\)
\(z^{(4)} = w^{(3)}a^{(3)}\)\(a^{(4)} = g\!\left(z^{(4)}\right)\)\(\hat y = a^{(4)}\)

The last weight

\(w^{(3)}\) reaches \(J\) through \(z^{(4)}\) then \(a^{(4)}\), so the chain rule gives three factors:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w^{(3)}} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial J}{\partial a^{(4)}}\times\frac{\partial a^{(4)}}{\partial z^{(4)}}}_{\textstyle E^{(4)}}\times\frac{\partial z^{(4)}}{\partial w^{(3)}}$$

The last factor is easy: \(z^{(4)} = w^{(3)}a^{(3)}\), so \(\partial z^{(4)}/\partial w^{(3)} = a^{(3)}\). The first two factors together are precisely \(\partial J/\partial z^{(4)}\), which is \(E^{(4)}\). Hence

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w^{(3)}} = E^{(4)} \times a^{(3)}$$

If we consider Binay Cross Entropy Loss, paired with Sigmoid activation function, like we did for Logistic Regression earlier, we get:

$$E^{(4)}=\left(\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial z^{(4)}}\right)=-\left(y-a^{(4)}\right)$$

The next weight back

\(w^{(2)}\) has a longer route, but most of it is the route we just walked:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w^{(2)}} = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial J}{\partial a^{(4)}}\times\frac{\partial a^{(4)}}{\partial z^{(4)}}\times\frac{\partial z^{(4)}}{\partial a^{(3)}}\times\frac{\partial a^{(3)}}{\partial z^{(3)}}\right)}_{\textstyle E^{(3)}}\times\;\frac{\partial z^{(3)}}{\partial w^{(2)}}$$

which is the same shape as before, \(\partial J/\partial w^{(2)} = E^{(3)} \times a^{(2)}\). Expanding the bracket shows how \(E^{(3)}\) relates to \(E^{(4)}\): the first two factors are \(E^{(4)}\), the third is \(\partial z^{(4)}/\partial a^{(3)} = w^{(3)}\), and the fourth is \(g'\!\left(z^{(3)}\right)\). So

$$E^{(3)} = E^{(4)} \times w^{(3)} \times g'\!\left(z^{(3)}\right)$$

Repeating the argument one layer further gives:

$$E^{(2)} = E^{(3)} \times w^{(2)} \times g'\!\left(z^{(2)}\right)$$ $$\partial J/\partial w^{(1)} = E^{(2)} \times a^{(1)}$$
8

The two recursions

Backpropagation in full, for the scalar case. Every later result is a re-reading of these two lines.

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial w^{(l)}} \;=\; {\color{#B23A6B}{E^{(l+1)}}} \;\times\; {\color{#3B528B}{a^{(l)}}}$$
E(l+1)Error signal arriving from the next layer — how wrong the thing this weight feeds turned out to be
a(l)Activation this weight carried forward — how much this weight actually contributed on this example

A weight's gradient is large only when both factors are large: the downstream unit must be substantially wrong, and this weight must have been carrying a substantial signal. A weight that transmitted nothing on this example gets no update from it, however wrong the output was.

$${\color{#4A1E5C}{E^{(l)}}} \;=\; {\color{#B23A6B}{E^{(l+1)}}} \;\times\; {\color{#1F8A85}{w^{(l)}}} \;\times\; {\color{#9A8B1E}{g'\!\left(z^{(l)}\right)}}$$
E(l)Error signal for the current layer, ready to be reused one layer further back
E(l+1)What arrived from the layer ahead
w(l)Routes the blame back along the connection that carried the signal forward
g′(z(l))Scales it by how responsive this unit is at its current operating point

The second equation is the one that matters for Part C. It is applied once per layer, so travelling back through \(L\) layers multiplies the error by \(L\) copies of \(g'\). Whatever \(g'\) typically is, that value gets raised to the power of the depth — and block 14 works out the consequences.

The weight gradient uses \(E^{(l+1)}\) but the error recursion uses \(g'\!\left(z^{(l)}\right)\). Why do the layer indices differ?

Because they answer different questions. \(\partial J/\partial w^{(l)}\) asks how wrong the unit this weight feeds into was, which lives in layer \(l+1\). The recursion asks how sensitive the unit this weight comes from is, which lives in layer \(l\). Mixing the two up is the most common slip in hand-worked backpropagation.

9

The Hadamard product

A small piece of notation, needed because one term in the recursion is element-wise and the other is not.

For two matrices of identical shape, the Hadamard product multiplies corresponding entries:

$$C_{m\times n} = A_{m\times n} \odot B_{m\times n}, \qquad C_{ij} = A_{ij}\,B_{ij}$$
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}1&5\\3&-2\end{bmatrix}\;\Longrightarrow\; C=\begin{bmatrix}1&10\\9&-8\end{bmatrix}$$

It is needed because \(g\) is applied separately to each unit. Unit \(i\)'s error must be scaled by unit \(i\)'s own \(g'\!\left(z_i\right)\) and by nobody else's — which is elementwise multiplication, not a matrix product. The weight term, by contrast, genuinely mixes units together and stays a matrix product.

10

Generalised vector form

The same two recursions with real layers instead of single units. Only the bookkeeping changes.

With \(|l| = m\) and \(|l+1| = n\):

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial W^{(l)}} \;=\; {\color{#B23A6B}{\vec E^{(l+1)}}} \;\times\; {\color{#3B528B}{\vec a^{(l)\top}}}$$
Result — (n × m)One number per weight, matching the shape of \(W^{(l)}\) exactly
Error vector — (n × 1)One entry per receiving unit
Activation row — (1 × m)One entry per sending unit

A column times a row is an outer product, and it produces an entire matrix in one operation: entry \((i,j)\) is \(E^{(l+1)}_i a^{(l)}_j\), which is exactly the scalar rule of block 8 applied to the weight joining unit \(j\) to unit \(i\). All \(mn\) gradients fall out of a single multiplication.

$${\color{#4A1E5C}{\vec E^{(l)}}} \;=\; \Bigl({\color{#1F8A85}{W^{(l)\top}\vec E^{(l+1)}}}\Bigr) \;\odot\; {\color{#9A8B1E}{g'\!\left(\vec z^{(l)}\right)}}$$
Result — (m × 1)Error for the current layer
Routing — (m × n)(n × 1)The transpose sends blame backwards along the forward connections
Sensitivity — (m × 1)Element-wise, one derivative per unit of layer \(l\)

The transpose is not a trick of notation. In the forward direction \(W^{(l)}\) maps \(m\) units to \(n\); going backwards means mapping \(n\) error entries to \(m\), and \(W^{(l)\top}\) is the \((m\times n)\) matrix that does it. A unit that fed strongly into many downstream units receives correspondingly more blame back.

Shape check as a debugging tool

Almost every implementation bug in hand-written backpropagation is a shape error, and the shapes over-determine the formula. If \(\partial J/\partial W^{(l)}\) does not come out \((n\times m)\), the expression is wrong regardless of how plausible it looks. Writing the dimensions under every term, as the lecture slides do, catches the mistake before any numbers are computed.

The bias gradient, follows from the same derivation with \(\partial z^{(l+1)}/\partial b^{(l)} = 1\):

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial \vec b^{(l)}} = \vec E^{(l+1)}$$
11

Error at the output layer

Everything so far propagates an error that already exists. The chain has to start at the output, where \(E^{(L)} = \partial J/\partial z^{(L)}\) is computed directly from the loss.

For binary cross-entropy with a sigmoid output — the algebra is unusually clean. With \(J = -\left[y\log a + (1-y)\log(1-a)\right]\) and \(a = \sigma(z)\):

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial a} = \frac{a-y}{a(1-a)}, \qquad \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} = a(1-a)$$

The two factors cancel completely:

$$E^{(L)} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial z^{(L)}} = a^{(L)} - y = -\left(y - a^{(L)}\right)$$

This cancellation is the reason cross-entropy is paired with sigmoid rather than squared error. With squared error the \(a(1-a)\) term survives, so a confidently wrong output: \(a \approx 0\) when \(y = 1\) : produces a vanishing gradient exactly when the largest correction is needed. Cross-entropy gives an unbounded gradient there instead.

TaskOutput activationLoss\(E^{(L)}\)
Binary classificationSigmoidBinary cross-entropy\(\hat y - y\)
Multi-class, one labelSoftmaxCategorical cross-entropy\(\hat{\vec y} - \vec y\)
Multi-labelSigmoid, per outputSum of binary cross-entropies\(\hat{\vec y} - \vec y\)
RegressionNone (identity)Mean squared error\(\hat{\vec y} - \vec y\)

All four rows give the same expression. That is not a coincidence — each pairing is chosen precisely so the activation derivative cancels against the loss derivative, which is why these combinations are the standard ones.

12

Worked example: GATE DA 2025

Six partial derivatives through a ReLU network, computed by forward pass then backward pass.

Forward pass

With \(u = 2\), \(v = 3\) and the weights shown:

QuantityExpressionValue
\(z_1\)\(a\,u + b\,v = 1(2) + 1(3)\)\(5\)
\(g_1\)\(\mathrm{ReLU}(5)\)\(5\)
\(z_2\)\(c\,u + d\,v = 1(2) + (-1)(3)\)\(-1\)
\(g_2\)\(\mathrm{ReLU}(-1)\)\(0\)
\(z_3\)\(e\,g_1 + f\,g_2 = 4(5) + 1(0)\)\(20\)
\(y = g_3\)\(\mathrm{ReLU}(20)\)\(20\)

The single fact that decides half the answers is \(z_2 = -1\). The lower unit is in its flat region, so \(\mathrm{ReLU}'(z_2) = 0\) and nothing downstream of it can be influenced by \(c\) or \(d\).

Backward pass

Each local derivative, evaluated at the forward-pass values:

DerivativeReasonValue
\(\partial y/\partial z_3\)\(\mathrm{ReLU}'(20)\), and \(20 > 0\)\(1\)
\(\partial z_3/\partial g_1\)coefficient \(e\)\(4\)
\(\partial z_3/\partial g_2\)coefficient \(f\)\(1\)
\(\partial g_1/\partial z_1\)\(\mathrm{ReLU}'(5)\), and \(5 > 0\)\(1\)
\(\partial g_2/\partial z_2\)\(\mathrm{ReLU}'(-1)\), and \(-1 < 0\)\(0\)
\(\partial z_1/\partial a,\ \partial z_2/\partial c\)the input \(u\)\(2\)
\(\partial z_1/\partial b,\ \partial z_2/\partial d\)the input \(v\)\(3\)
\(\partial z_3/\partial e\)the activation \(g_1\)\(5\)
\(\partial z_3/\partial f\)the activation \(g_2\)\(0\)

Multiplying out

GradientChainResult
\(\partial y/\partial a\)\(1 \times 4 \times 1 \times 2\)\(8\)
\(\partial y/\partial b\)\(1 \times 4 \times 1 \times 3\)\(12\)
\(\partial y/\partial c\)\(1 \times 1 \times {\color{#B23A6B}{0}} \times 2\)\(0\)
\(\partial y/\partial d\)\(1 \times 1 \times {\color{#B23A6B}{0}} \times 3\)\(0\)
\(\partial y/\partial e\)\(1 \times 5\)\(5\)
\(\partial y/\partial f\)\(1 \times {\color{#B23A6B}{0}}\)\(0\)

Three of the six gradients are zero, and a gradient of zero means no update. If the lower unit stays in its negative region across the whole training set, \(c\), \(d\) and \(f\) are frozen permanently — the dying ReLU problem of block 17, visible here in a network small enough to check by hand.

If \(u\) were \(4\) instead of \(2\), which of the six answers would change, and why?

All of them. \(z_2 = 1(4) + (-1)(3) = 1 > 0\), so the lower unit switches on: \(\partial g_2/\partial z_2\) becomes \(1\), and \(\partial y/\partial c\), \(\partial y/\partial d\), \(\partial y/\partial f\) become \(4\), \(3\) and \(1\) respectively. The upper path changes too, since \(z_1 = 7\) and \(g_1 = 7\), giving \(\partial y/\partial a = 16\), \(\partial y/\partial b = 12\), \(\partial y/\partial e = 7\). Which units are active is part of the input, not a fixed property of the network.

Part C
Activation functions
13

Sigmoid

The historical default. Its two weaknesses are both consequences of the backward recursion, not of the function's shape as such.

$$\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}, \qquad \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\bigl(1-\sigma(z)\bigr)$$

The derivative is worth deriving once, because the self-referential form is what makes sigmoid cheap to differentiate — the forward pass has already computed \(\sigma(z)\), so no new exponentials are needed:

$$\sigma'(z) = \frac{d}{dz}\left(1+e^{-z}\right)^{-1} = \frac{e^{-z}}{\left(1+e^{-z}\right)^{2}} = \sigma(z)\bigl(1-\sigma(z)\bigr)$$

Maximising \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\) over \(\sigma \in (0,1)\) gives \(\sigma = 0.5\), so the largest possible derivative is \(0.25\). This ceiling is the single most consequential number in the lecture.

Region\(\sigma(z)\)\(\sigma'(z)\)Gradient strength
\(z \ll 0\)\(\approx 0\)\(\approx 0\)Vanishing — unit is saturated
\(z \approx 0\)\(\approx 0.5\)\(\approx 0.25\)Best case, and still a quarter
\(z \gg 0\)\(\approx 1\)\(\approx 0\)Vanishing — unit is saturated
In its favour
  • Smooth and differentiable everywhere
  • Output in \((0,1)\) reads directly as a probability, which is what makes it the right output unit for binary classification
  • Pairs with cross-entropy so that \(E^{(L)} = \hat y - y\) (block 11)
Against
  • Saturates at both ends, so \(\sigma' \to 0\) for most inputs
  • \(\sigma' \leq 0.25\) even at its best, shrinking gradients at every layer
  • Output is never negative, forcing all weights into a neuron to move together (block 15)
  • \(e^{-z}\) is more expensive than a comparison against zero

  • The first two objections are about depth and are developed in block 14
  • The third is about the direction of updates and is developed in block 15
  • Neither applies to a single-layer model, which is why sigmoid remains fine in logistic regression and as an output unit, and poor as a hidden activation.

14

Vanishing gradients

What repeated application of the error recursion does to a number smaller than one.

Apply the recursion of block 10 three times and the nesting becomes visible:

$$\vec E^{(l)} = \left(W^{(l)\top}\!\left(W^{(l+1)\top}\!\left(W^{(l+2)\top}\vec E^{(l+3)} \odot g'\!\bigl(\vec z^{(l+2)}\bigr)\right)\odot g'\!\bigl(\vec z^{(l+1)}\bigr)\right)\right)\odot g'\!\bigl(\vec z^{(l)}\bigr)$$

Each layer contributes one factor of \(g'\) and one of \(W^{\top}\). For sigmoid every \(g'\) lies in \((0,\,0.25]\), so travelling back through \(L\) layers multiplies the error by a product of \(L\) numbers, none larger than a quarter. Even in the best case:

$$\underbrace{0.25 \times 0.25 \times \cdots \times 0.25}_{L \text{ layers}} = 0.25^{\,L}$$

At ten layers that is \(\approx 10^{-6}\); at twenty, \(\approx 10^{-12}\). The early layers receive a gradient indistinguishable from zero and effectively stop training, while the layers near the output continue to learn — so the network trains, badly, using only its last few layers.

Important Note:

A common misconception is that the problem of vanishing gradients is often entirely attributed to \(g'\), concluding that "repeatedly multiplying with such small values drives the product to 0". The product actually involves \(W^{(l)\top}g'\!\left(\vec z^{(l)}\right)\) at every step, so what decays or grows is governed by \(\lVert W\rVert \cdot g'\), not \(g'\) alone.

Initialising weights so that \(\lVert W\rVert \cdot g' \approx 1\) keeps the product near unity for many layers. It is also why ReLU networks can explode despite having \(g'=1\): with \(g'\) fixed, \(\lVert W\rVert\) alone decides the outcome.

Residual connections add an identity path, \(a^{(l+1)} = g\!\left(z^{(l+1)}\right) + a^{(l)}\). Why does that help?

Differentiating the identity path gives a term of exactly \(1\) added to the recursion, so the error signal has a route backwards that is never multiplied by \(g'\) at all. The product can no longer decay geometrically with depth, which is what made networks of hundreds of layers trainable.

15

Outputs that are not zero-centred

A second, independent problem with sigmoid: it constrains the direction of every update, not just its size.

From block 8, the gradient of a single weight is

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial W^{(l)}_{ij}} = E^{(l+1)}_i \times a^{(l)}_j$$

Sigmoid activations are always positive, so \(a^{(l)}_j > 0\) always. The sign of the gradient is therefore decided entirely by \(E^{(l+1)}_i\) — which does not depend on \(j\). Every weight feeding into unit \(i\) consequently shares one sign, and they all increase together or all decrease together on any given step.

Shared Gradient Direction for Weights

The gradient of a single weight feeding into unit $i$ is given by:
$$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial W_{ij}^{(l)}} = E_i^{(l+1)} \times a_j^{(l)} $$
Because Sigmoid activations are always positive ($a_j^{(l)} > 0$), the sign of the gradient is entirely decided by the error term $E_i^{(l+1)}$. Consequently, all weights feeding into unit $i$ (highlighted above) share the same sign, meaning they will all increase together or decrease together on any given update step.
Important difference: per neuron, NOT per layer

Students often conclude that "gradient of all weights at a particular level will have the same sign, all of them will move one way". The derivation supports something narrower. Only \(a^{(l)}_j\) is guaranteed positive; \(E^{(l+1)}_i\) varies freely with \(i\). So the shared sign holds across all weights entering one receiving unit, while different units in the same layer can have errors of opposite sign and move in opposite directions.

Why that costs speed

Suppose the optimum requires \(w_1\) to increase and \(w_2\) to decrease. With both gradients locked to one sign, that move is unavailable in a single step. The optimiser must overshoot in one direction and correct in the next step, tracing a staircase towards a target it could have approached directly.

The lecture's numerical example

Two identical networks, target weights \(w_{opt} = [1,\,-1]\), current weights \(w = [0.2,\,0.6]\), learning rate \(\alpha = 0.1\). The only difference is the sign of the second activation.

StepSigmoid: \(a = [0.8,\ 0.9]\)Tanh: \(a = [0.8,\ -0.9]\)
Prediction \(\hat y = w^{\top}a\)\(0.2(0.8)+0.6(0.9) = 0.7\)\(0.2(0.8)+0.6(-0.9) = -0.38\)
Target \(y = w_{opt}^{\top}a\)\(1(0.8)+(-1)(0.9) = -0.1\)\(1(0.8)+(-1)(-0.9) = 1.7\)
Error \(e = \hat y - y\)\(0.7-(-0.1) = 0.8\)\(-0.38-1.7 = -2.08\)
\(\partial J/\partial w_1 = e\,a_1\)\(0.8(0.8) = 0.64\)\(-2.08(0.8) = -1.664\)
\(\partial J/\partial w_2 = e\,a_2\)\(0.8(0.9) = 0.72\)\(-2.08(-0.9) = 1.872\)
\(w_{new} = w - \alpha\nabla\)\([0.136,\ 0.528]\)\([0.3664,\ 0.4128]\)
Direction of \(w_1\) (wants \(\uparrow\))decreasedincreased
Direction of \(w_2\) (wants \(\downarrow\))decreaseddecreased

Both gradients came out positive in the sigmoid column, so both weights fell — including \(w_1\), which needed to rise towards \(1\). In the tanh column the negative activation flipped one sign, and both weights moved the right way on the very first step.

16

Hyperbolic tangent

Sigmoid rescaled to span \([-1,1]\). It fixes the zero-centring problem completely and the vanishing gradient problem only partially.

$$\tanh(z) = \frac{e^{z}-e^{-z}}{e^{z}+e^{-z}}, \qquad \frac{d}{dz}\tanh(z) = 1-\tanh^{2}(z)$$

Tanh is a stretched sigmoid: \(\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z)-1\). That rescaling does two things. It makes the output symmetric about zero, so activations can be negative and the sign-locking of block 15 disappears. And it raises the maximum derivative from \(0.25\) to \(1\), so the error signal is no longer guaranteed to shrink at every layer.

Region\(\tanh(z)\)\(\tanh'(z)\)Gradient strength
\(z \ll 0\)\(\approx -1\)\(\approx 0\)Vanishing
\(z \approx 0\)\(\approx z\)\(\approx 1\)Strong
\(z \gg 0\)\(\approx +1\)\(\approx 0\)Vanishing

The middle row also explains why tanh behaves well near initialization: for small \(z\), \(\tanh(z) \approx z\), so an untrained network is close to linear and gradients pass through almost unchanged.

What is fixed and what is not

Saturation remains. Both tails are still flat, so a unit driven to a large \(\lvert z\rvert\) still contributes \(g' \approx 0\) and still blocks the error signal. Tanh raises the ceiling and removes the sign constraint; it does not remove the floor. This is why tanh delayed rather than solved the depth problem, and why ReLU displaced it.

17

Rectified linear unit

The one that made deep networks trainable, by giving up smoothness and boundedness in exchange for a derivative that is exactly one.

$$\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0,z), \qquad \mathrm{ReLU}'(z) = \begin{cases}1 & z > 0\\ 0 & z \leq 0\end{cases}$$

The derivative at \(z = 0\) does not exist; implementations pick \(0\) by convention. This is harmless in practice, since \(z\) is exactly zero with probability zero for continuous inputs.

In its favour
  • No vanishing gradient on the active side. \(g' = 1\), so the error signal passes through undiminished — the property that made very deep networks trainable
  • Cheap. A comparison and a select, against an exponential for sigmoid and tanh
  • Sparse activations. Negative pre-activations output exactly zero, so only a subset of units is active for any given input
  • Sparsity has a natural reading: an activation measures how strongly a feature is detected, and "\(-3\) units of cat" means nothing — either some cat evidence is present or none is
Against
  • Dying ReLU. A unit stuck at \(z \leq 0\) for every input has \(g' = 0\) always, so its weights never update again
  • Unbounded above. Activations can grow without limit, which compounds across layers
  • Not zero-centred. Outputs are \(\geq 0\), so the sign-locking of block 15 applies here too
  • Discards sign information. Every negative pre-activation maps to the same zero

The dying ReLU problem

This is the failure mode the GATE question in block 12 exhibits. Once a unit's weights and bias put \(z \leq 0\) for the entire training set, its gradient is zero on every example, so nothing can move it back. The unit is permanently dead — not slow, not saturated, but removed from the network.

The lecture lists three causes, all of which push \(z\) permanently negative:

  • A learning rate that is too high. One oversized update can move the bias far enough negative that the unit never activates again. This is the most common cause in practice.
  • Poor initialization. Weights drawn too negative, or a bias initialised at or below zero, can start a unit dead.
  • Skewed inputs. If the inputs are mostly negative and unnormalised, many units begin in the flat region.

Unbounded outputs

The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function permits, rather than directly causes, unbounded growth in neural network outputs and gradients because its positive branch lacks an upper mathematical limit.

The mechanics of this phenomenon break down into the following distinct concepts:

1. The Unbounded Forward Pass

For positive inputs, ReLU acts purely as an identity function ($f(x) = x$). Unlike sigmoid or tanh activations, which forcibly squash or "clip" large numbers into a constrained range (e.g., $[0, 1]$ or $[-1, 1]$), ReLU passes large positive numbers forward exactly as they are. This allows activation values to compound and grow progressively larger layer after layer.

2. The Link to Exploding Gradients

During backpropagation, the gradient of the loss with respect to a weight is calculated as the product of the error ($E$) and the input activation ($a$). This relationship is expressed mathematically as:

$$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = E \cdot a $$

Because the activation value $a$ is a direct multiplier here, any massive, unbounded activations generated in the forward pass will inherently produce massively inflated gradients during the backward pass.

3. Permission vs. Causation

ReLU itself does not force values to explode; it merely removes the ceiling that would otherwise stop them. The actual determining factor of whether activations and gradients explode is the scale of the network's weights. If the weights are too large, their repeated multiplication through the layers acts as the engine driving the explosion, while ReLU simply leaves the door open.

4. Distinct Phenomena and Solutions

Exploding activations (forward pass) and exploding gradients (backward pass) are related but mathematically distinct problems requiring targeted solutions:

  • Proper Weight Initialization: This addresses the root cause by mathematically scaling the starting weights so the signal variance remains stable, preventing activations from growing out of control.
  • Gradient Clipping: This serves as a secondary failsafe, artificially capping the maximum allowable size of the gradients during backpropagation regardless of how large the forward activations became.
18

Leaky ReLU and the smooth family

Giving the negative region a small non-zero slope, and then — the functions that replaced Leaky ReLU in practice.

$$\mathrm{LeakyReLU}(z) = \begin{cases}z & z \geq 0\\ \alpha z & z < 0\end{cases}, \qquad \mathrm{LeakyReLU}'(z) = \begin{cases}1 & z > 0\\ \alpha & z < 0\end{cases}$$

Because \(g' = \alpha > 0\) everywhere, a unit in its negative region still receives gradient and can climb back out. Negative pre-activations also retain some information rather than collapsing to a single zero, which matters when the sign is meaningful — sentiment that can be positive or negative, or physical quantities where negative values are real.

The cost is one more hyperparameter. Too small an \(\alpha\) behaves like ReLU and can still stall; too large and the function drifts towards linearity, weakening the non-linearity the network needs. PReLU removes the guesswork by learning \(\alpha\) as a parameter.

Parametric ReLU

PReLU stands for Parametric Rectified Linear Unit. It is an advanced variation of Leaky ReLU that allows the neural network to learn the optimal activation shape on its own.

The defining difference lies entirely in how that negative slope ($\alpha$) is determined:

  • Leaky ReLU: The slope $\alpha$ is a fixed, hardcoded constant (e.g., $0.01$) chosen by the engineer before training begins. It never changes.
  • PReLU: The slope $\alpha$ is a learnable parameter. The network starts with an initial value for $\alpha$ (often $0.25$), and during backpropagation, it calculates the gradient of the loss with respect to $\alpha$. The optimizer updates $\alpha$ on every step, right alongside the network's regular weights and biases.

Smooth alternatives

Leaky ReLU keeps ReLU's hinge at the origin. Three widely used functions smooth it away:

NameDefinitionProperty it adds
Exponential Linear Unit\(z\) if \(z>0\), else \(\alpha\left(e^{z}-1\right)\)Saturates to \(-\alpha\) rather than growing, so negative outputs stay bounded; pushes the mean activation towards zero
Gaussian Error Linear Unit\(z\,\Phi(z)\), with \(\Phi\) the normal CDFWeights the input by the probability it exceeds a random threshold; the default in transformer architectures
Swish / Sigmoid Linear Unit\(z\,\sigma(z)\)Non-monotone — dips slightly below zero before rising — which empirically helps in deep networks
What to reach for first

ReLU remains the sensible default for hidden layers in ordinary feedforward and convolutional networks: it is the cheapest and, with sound initialization and a reasonable learning rate, dying units are rarely a serious problem. Move to Leaky ReLU or ELU if you diagnose dead units; use GELU in transformer-style architectures, where it is the convention.

19

Choosing one

All four on the same axes, and the summary that follows from them.

SigmoidTanhReLULeaky ReLU
Range\((0,1)\)\((-1,1)\)\([0,\infty)\)\((-\infty,\infty)\)
Max \(g'\)\(0.25\)\(1\)\(1\)\(1\)
Zero-centredNoYesNoRoughly
SaturatesBoth sidesBoth sidesNegative side onlyNeither side
Can units die?NoNoYesNo
CostExponentialExponentialComparisonComparison
Use as hidden unitAvoidAcceptable, shallow nets and RNNsDefaultWhen units die
Use as output unitBinary / multi-labelRarelyRegression, non-negative targetsRarely
The table says avoid sigmoid as a hidden unit, but block 11 recommends it as an output unit. Is that consistent?

Yes, because the objections are about depth and the output layer has no depth beneath it. Saturation hurts by multiplying \(g'\) once per layer as the error travels back; at the output layer \(g'\) is applied exactly once, and with cross-entropy it cancels out entirely. The zero-centring problem concerns activations fed forward into further weights, and an output layer feeds nothing forward.

Part D
Training dynamics
20

The problem with a fixed rate

One number multiplies every gradient in the network, and no single value is right for the whole of training.

$$w^{(k+1)} = w^{(k)} - \alpha\,\nabla_w J$$

Backpropagation supplies \(\nabla_w J\); \(\alpha\) decides how far to act on it. The two failure modes are opposite and equally fatal:

  • \(\alpha\) too large — each step overshoots, the weights oscillate across the minimum with growing amplitude, and the loss may diverge. This is also the most common way to kill ReLU units (block 17).
  • \(\alpha\) too small — progress is reliable but slow, and the run may stall in a poor region long before reaching anything good.

The deeper issue is that the right \(\alpha\) is not constant in time.

  • Early on the weights are far from any good region and large steps are efficient.
  • Later, near a minimum, the same large step bounces across the valley instead of settling into it.
A single fixed number cannot be right for both phases — hence decay.

21

Four decay schedules

Start large, finish small. The families differ in whether the reduction is abrupt or continuous, and how fast it compounds.

Step decay

$$\alpha_{curr} = \alpha_0 \cdot m^{\left\lfloor \frac{curr}{k} \right\rfloor}, \qquad 0 < m < 1$$
SymbolMeaning
\(\alpha_0\)Initial learning rate
\(m\)Drop factor — the fraction the rate is multiplied by at each drop, e.g. \(0.5\) halves it
\(k\)Number of epochs between drops
\(curr\)Current epoch
Step size \(k\)Drop factor \(m\)BehaviourConsequence
SmallSmall (\(\approx 0.5\))Frequent, large dropsVery aggressive — fast at first, then may underfit as the rate collapses early
SmallLarge (\(0.8\)–\(0.9\))Frequent, gentle dropsClose to smooth decay; controlled, a good default
LargeSmall (\(\approx 0.5\))Rare, large dropsLong stretches at one rate, then an abrupt change in behaviour at each drop
LargeLarge (\(0.8\)–\(0.9\))Rare, gentle dropsVery slow decay; needs a long run, fine on smooth landscapes

Smooth decay (inverse-time)

$$\alpha_{curr} = \frac{\alpha_0}{1 + d \cdot curr}$$

Continuous rather than stepped, with \(d\) the decay rate. The reduction is gentle: after \(T\) epochs the rate is divided by \(1 + dT\), which grows only linearly, so the rate decays as \(1/T\) and never collapses quickly.

Exponential decay

$$\alpha_{curr} = \alpha_0 \cdot e^{-d \cdot curr}$$

Also continuous, but multiplicative in the exponent, so it falls far faster than inverse-time for the same \(d\).

Performance-based decay

Performance-based decay is a reactive learning rate schedule that dynamically reduces the learning rate ($\alpha$) only when the model stops showing meaningful improvement on a validation dataset.

1. The Limitation of Fixed Schedules

Standard decay schedules reduce the learning rate based strictly on the current epoch number. Because they are programmed in advance, they are "blind" to the model's actual training state; they might prematurely reduce the learning rate while the model is still making rapid progress, or fail to reduce it when the model is stuck.

2. The Reactive Mechanism

Instead of predicting when the learning rate should drop, performance-based decay watches the data and reacts. The process relies on a continuous evaluation loop:

  • Monitor: After every training epoch, the system evaluates and records the validation loss.
  • Evaluate (Patience & Threshold): The system checks if the loss has improved by at least a predefined minimum amount (the threshold). It will tolerate a lack of improvement for a specific number of consecutive epochs (the patience).
  • Decay (Factor): If the loss fails to improve by the threshold before the patience runs out, the current learning rate $\alpha$ is multiplied by a reduction factor (typically a value between $0.1$ and $0.5$).
  • Reset: The patience counter is reset to zero, and training continues with the newly reduced learning rate.
3. The Signature Pattern

This method produces a distinct cause-and-effect pattern during training: a drop in the learning rate is exclusively triggered by the validation loss flattening out (hitting a plateau). Dropping the learning rate at this exact moment allows the optimizer to take finer steps and settle deeper into the local minimum, which is typically followed by a secondary, sudden fall in the validation loss.

4. The Trade-offs

While this data-driven approach is highly effective, it introduces specific costs to the training pipeline:

  • It inherently requires a dedicated validation set to monitor unseen data performance.
  • It forces the engineer to manually configure three new hyperparameters: patience, threshold, and factor.

In the provided figure, the learning rate ($\alpha$) remains a perfectly straight, horizontal line because the condition to reduce it has not yet been met during the plotted epochs.

Based on the mechanics of performance-based decay, here is why this happens:

  • Continuous Improvement: The defining rule of this schedule is that the learning rate only drops when the model stops improving. If you look at the validation loss (the blue line), it is steadily and consistently decreasing across the entire graph.
  • Patience Not Exceeded: Because the validation loss never flattens out into a plateau, the "patience" counter never runs out. The system sees that the current learning rate is still driving progress effectively.
  • Resulting Constant Rate: Since the trigger condition (a lack of progress) never occurs in this specific window, the learning rate remains exactly at its starting value ($0.100$) for the duration of the visible training period. It will only drop if the blue line eventually levels off.
22

Weight initialization

Block 14 established that the error signal is multiplied by \(W^{(l)\top}\) and \(g'\) at every layer. Initialization sets the scale of \(W\) at the start, and therefore decides whether that product begins near \(1\) or heads towards \(0\) or \(\infty\).

Two rules are standard, both derived by requiring the variance of the activations to be preserved from layer to layer:

NameVarianceUse withReasoning
Xavier / Glorot\(\operatorname{Var}(w) = \dfrac{2}{n_{in}+n_{out}}\)tanh, sigmoidBalances the forward and backward passes for an activation that is roughly linear near zero
He\(\operatorname{Var}(w) = \dfrac{2}{n_{in}}\)ReLU and variantsReLU zeroes half its inputs, halving the variance; the factor of \(2\) compensates

The Base Math (Where the fractions come from)

Let’s look at a single neuron. It takes a bunch of inputs (\(x\)), multiplies them by weights (\(w\)), and sums them up to get an output (\(y\)):

\(y = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dots + w_nx_n\)

In statistics, if you assume your inputs and weights are independent and centered around zero, the variance of their product is \(\text{Var}(w) \times \text{Var}(x)\). Because we are adding up \(n\) of these connections (where \(n\) is your number of inputs, or \(n_{in}\)), the total variance of the output becomes:

\(\text{Var}(y) = n_{in} \cdot \text{Var}(w) \cdot \text{Var}(x)\)

Remember our goal: we want the output variance to equal the input variance so the signal doesn't explode or die. So, we set \(\text{Var}(y) = \text{Var}(x)\):

\(\text{Var}(x) = n_{in} \cdot \text{Var}(w) \cdot \text{Var}(x)\)

Divide both sides by \(\text{Var}(x)\) and you get:

\(1 = n_{in} \cdot \text{Var}(w)\)

\(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{1}{n_{in}}\)

This is the foundational math: to keep a signal perfectly stable, the variance of your initial weights must be 1 divided by the number of incoming connections.

Where Xavier/Glorot Came From

In 2010, Xavier Glorot looked at that base math and realized a problem: a network has a forward pass (where data flows through \(n_{in}\)) and a backward pass (where gradients flow backward through \(n_{out}\)).

  • To keep the forward pass stable, you need \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{1}{n_{in}}\).
  • To keep the backward pass stable, you need \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{1}{n_{out}}\).

If a layer has 100 inputs and 500 outputs, you can't satisfy both equations at once. Xavier's solution was simply to compromise. He took the average of the two requirements:

\(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{in} + n_{out}}\)

This works brilliantly, but it makes one massive assumption: it assumes the activation function is linear (which Tanh and Sigmoid roughly are, right near zero).

Where He Initialization Came From

In 2015, Kaiming He realized that Xavier initialization was causing deep networks with ReLU to fail.

ReLU is \(f(x) = \max(0, x)\). It literally takes any negative number and turns it into zero. This means that as a signal passes through a ReLU layer, exactly half of the data is deleted. If you throw away half the data, you are throwing away half the variance.

If you use Xavier's math with ReLU, the variance equation actually looks like this because of that 50% data loss:

\(\text{Var}(y) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot n_{in} \cdot \text{Var}(w) \cdot \text{Var}(x)\)

If you set \(\text{Var}(y) = \text{Var}(x)\) again to try and keep the signal stable, you get:

\(1 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot n_{in} \cdot \text{Var}(w)\)

When you solve for \(\text{Var}(w)\), you have to multiply both sides by 2:

\(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{in}}\)

That is where He Initialization comes from. The 2 on top isn't a random magic number; it is a mathematical compensation. You are intentionally initializing the weights to be twice as large to perfectly offset the fact that ReLU is going to immediately destroy half of your signal.

Both of these formulas solve the exact same physics problem in deep learning: preventing the variance of a signal from exploding to infinity or vanishing to zero as it passes through multiple layers.

To keep a signal stable, the baseline mathematical requirement is that the variance of the weights must equal 1 divided by the number of connections (\(1/n\)). These two formulas are specific adaptations of that baseline rule.

1. Xavier / Glorot Initialization

The formula is defined as \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{in} + n_{out}}\). This equation was derived to balance the competing needs of the network's forward and backward passes when using symmetric activation functions like Tanh or Sigmoid.

  • The Conflict: During the forward pass, data flows through the input connections, meaning stability requires \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{1}{n_{in}}\). However, during backpropagation, gradients flow backward through the output connections, meaning stability requires \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{1}{n_{out}}\).
  • The Compromise: If a layer has 100 inputs and 500 outputs, you cannot satisfy both \(\frac{1}{100}\) and \(\frac{1}{500}\) simultaneously. Xavier Glorot's solution was to calculate the average number of connections for that layer: \(\frac{n_{in} + n_{out}}{2}\).
  • The Derivation: By substituting this average into the baseline \(1/n\) rule, you get \(\frac{1}{\frac{n_{in} + n_{out}}{2}}\). When you flip the fraction to simplify it, it becomes exactly \(\frac{2}{n_{in} + n_{out}}\).

2. He Initialization

The formula is defined as \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{in}}\). This equation was derived specifically to fix the catastrophic failure of Xavier initialization when applied to ReLU networks.

  • The Variance Loss: ReLU (\(\max(0, x)\)) blocks all negative numbers, effectively acting as a filter that permanently deletes exactly half of the signal. If you delete 50% of the data, you inherently destroy 50% of the variance.
  • The Mathematical Fix: If you use the standard baseline formula (\(1/n_{in}\)), the ReLU activation will instantly cut the resulting variance in half, causing the signal to decay and vanish over multiple layers. To perfectly offset this 50% destruction, Kaiming He proved you must intentionally inject twice as much variance at the starting line.
  • The Derivation: You take the baseline requirement for the forward pass (\(\frac{1}{n_{in}}\)) and explicitly multiply it by 2 to counterbalance the ReLU filter, resulting directly in \(\frac{2}{n_{in}}\). (He's research demonstrated that balancing the forward pass alone was sufficient to prevent gradients from vanishing, so the \(n_{out}\) term was dropped entirely).

Why is Xavier Preferred for Tanh and Sigmoid and He for ReLU Mathematically?

The mathematical preference for these initializations comes down to how the specific activation function alters the variance of the data passing through it, and how the formulas mathematically compensate for those alterations.

Xavier Initialization for Tanh and Sigmoid

  • The Mathematical Property: Xavier initialization is preferred for tanh and sigmoid because these activation functions are roughly linear near zero. When weights are initialized to be small, the pre-activation values fall directly into this linear region.
  • Variance Preservation: Because they act like a linear pass-through near zero, they do not inherently crop or destroy the distribution of the data.
  • The Goal: Since the activation function itself isn't destroying variance, the only mathematical challenge is balancing the flow of variance for both the forward pass (driven by the number of inputs, \(n_{in}\)) and the backward pass (driven by the number of outputs, \(n_{out}\)).
  • The Result: The formula \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{in} + n_{out}}\) averages the incoming and outgoing connections, successfully balancing both the forward and backward passes for an activation that preserves the data's shape.

He Initialization for ReLU

  • The Mathematical Property: He initialization is required for ReLU and its variants because ReLU operates by zeroing out half of its inputs (all negative values).
  • Variance Destruction: Mathematically, taking a zero-centered distribution and turning the entire negative half into absolute zeros cuts the variance of that distribution exactly in half. If Xavier initialization were used, this halving effect would compound at every layer, rapidly shrinking the signal to nothing.
  • The Goal: The mathematical goal is strictly to compensate for this 50% loss of variance.
  • The Result: The He formula \(\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{in}}\) explicitly places a factor of 2 in the numerator to double the starting variance of the weights. This factor of 2 perfectly compensates for the fact that ReLU halves the variance, holding the overall scale constant so the backward pass can survive.

Two further points the lecture's advice depends on:

  • Never initialise all weights to zero, or to any single constant. Every unit in a layer would then compute the same thing, receive the same gradient, and remain identical forever. Randomness is what breaks this symmetry — it is not merely a convenient default.
  • Initialise ReLU biases at zero or slightly positive. A small positive bias such as \(0.01\) starts every unit on the active side.
23

Batching and regularisation

How many examples per update

The gradient of \(J\) is an average over training examples. Computing it over all of them is exact but slow; computing it over a subset is noisy but cheap:

Batch size interacts with the learning rate: a larger batch gives a less noisy gradient, which supports a larger \(\alpha\). A common heuristic is to scale \(\alpha\) linearly with batch size, using warm-up (block 23) to survive the first few steps.

A different problem: overfitting

Everything in Part D so far concerns optimisation — reaching a low training loss. A network can succeed at that completely and still be useless, having memorised the training set. Three standard countermeasures:

  • \(L_2\) regularisation (weight decay). Add \(\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert w\rVert^2\) to the loss, which contributes \(\lambda w\) to every gradient and pulls weights towards zero.
  • Early stopping. Halt when the validation loss stops improving. It composes naturally with the plateau schedule of block 23, since both watch the same signal.
  • Dropout. Randomly switch off hidden units during training so no unit can depend on any other being present.
Two problems that look alike and are not

A model that will not fit the training data has an optimisation problem — look at the activation, the initialization, the learning rate. A model that fits the training data and fails on held-out data has a generalisation problem — look at regularisation and at the data itself. Changing the activation function will not fix overfitting, and dropout will not fix a vanishing gradient. Diagnosing which one you have, by comparing training loss against validation loss, comes before choosing a remedy.
